study.locator: 'Dolma Document Format' with the `id` field and the `metadata` field

focus: State the purpose before you filter: the behavior the model must have and the population it serves. Dolma scopes itself to English text on purpose and says that this reinforces English as the default (Section 3), which is what makes its English-only rules defensible.

A page reaches you through several hops, and each hop has its own rules: `robots.txt` and terms of service at crawl time, copyright and any license on the content, and the license on the collection that redistributes it. Keep one row per source and mark each field verified, assumed or unknown.

A collection license does not pass to the documents inside it, and a content license does not override a site's terms of service. The lecture's CommonPile list and the YouTube example make both points.

A deletion or takedown request can be honored only if the document id is stable across every later version and every derived artifact keeps it. Dolma requires this of the `id` field so that a blocklist applies to all versions.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the one-page ledger for a corpus you plan to build: a purpose statement of three or four lines (behavior, population, out-of-scope uses), then one row per source with `source`, `acquired_from`, `date`, `basis` (license, consent or exception claimed), `restrictions` (`robots.txt`, terms), `personal_data`, `deletion_contact` and `unknown`. Mark every cell verified, assumed or unknown, and list which cells you could not fill from the data alone.
traps: Treating 'it is in the crawl' as 'it may be used for training'. A crawl records how you obtained a page, not what its owner permits.

Writing the purpose as a list of sources ('web, code, books'). That gives you nothing to test filters against: Dodge Sections 5.2 and 5.3 show a blocklist removing text by and about minority groups, which counts as a loss only if those groups are in the population you stated.
Filling the rights record after the download. The date, the version of the terms and the `robots.txt` you saw at that time cannot be rebuilt later, so capture them while acquiring.

selfTest.q: A page is in the crawl snapshot you downloaded. Give two separate reasons you may still be unable to train on it.
selfTest.a: The owner holds copyright unless a license or an exception such as fair use applies, and that exception is unsettled. Independently, the site's terms of service or `robots.txt` can restrict automated copying even when the content is licensed, and the page may contain personal data.

selfTest.q: Why must a document id stay the same from the raw files to every later dataset version?
selfTest.a: A blocklist for takedown requests, evaluation leaks or manual rejection is a list of ids. If ids were reassigned per version, the list would stop matching the later versions without any error, and a deleted document could survive in them.

selfTest.q: A corpus is released under a permissive collection license. Can you assume each document in it is free to use?
selfTest.a: No. The collection license covers the compilation. Each document keeps whatever status its owner gave it, so you still need a per-source basis, and laundering of copyrighted work into a permissive collection is a known risk.

selfTest.q: A corpus is scoped to English on purpose. Name one thing that scope justifies and one claim it does not support.
selfTest.a: It justifies English-specific rules such as a stop-word test or an English language-ID threshold. It does not support any claim about how a model trained on it behaves in other languages, and the scope should be stated in the card so readers do not infer one.

study.title: Resiliparse: HTML2Text and FastWARC
study.locator: HTML2Text sections 'Basic Plain Text Conversion' and 'Main Content Extraction'; then the FastWARC page at https://resiliparse.chatnoir.eu/en/stable/man/fastwarc.html, sections 'Iterating WARC Files', 'Filtering Records', 'Record Properties' and 'Freezing Records' (page read 2026-10-16, Resiliparse and FastWARC 1.0.9)

focus: A WARC file interleaves record types. Only `response` records hold a page; `request`, `warcinfo` and `metadata` records are not documents. Select the type when you open the iterator.

The document identity comes from the WARC header: `record_id` is the `WARC-Record-ID`, and the target URI and date sit beside it. Write them next to the text at the moment you extract, because nothing later can recover them.

Extraction is lossy and a choice, not a fact. With `main_content=False` (the default) `extract_plain_text` keeps navigation and footer text; with `main_content=True` it removes them, and it can also remove short real text such as list items and captions. FineWeb found WET text retained too much menu text and that extraction changed the trained model.
Bytes come first. Try UTF-8, fall back to `detect_encoding`, and keep the encoding you used in the record, since a wrong guess produces plausible but damaged text.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `extract_records(warc_path)` that opens the file with FastWARC, keeps only `response` records, decodes the body (UTF-8 first, then the detected encoding), calls `extract_plain_text`, and yields a dict with `record_id`, `url`, `date`, `encoding` and `text`. On a WARC you build with three response records and one request record, show that you get three documents and that `record_id` matches the header. Then run one page with `main_content=False` and `True` and write down one piece of text the second setting removed correctly and, if you can find one, one it removed wrongly.
traps: Passing the course test and believing boilerplate is gone. The fixture's expected text equals the default output (`main_content=False`), and with `main_content=True` it no longer matches, so the test checks decoding and plain-text conversion, not boilerplate removal. Measure that separately on pages you read.
Reading `record.reader.read()` twice. The reader is a live stream, so the second call returns empty bytes; call `freeze()` first if you need the payload again.

Storing documents as one text file and treating each line as a document. Extracted pages contain newlines, so the handout's tokenization starter, which adds the end-of-text token after every line, would insert document boundaries inside documents. Store one JSON object per document and tokenize each document as a unit.

selfTest.q: A WARC file has 10 records: 1 `warcinfo`, 4 `request` and 5 `response`. How many documents should extraction produce, and where does each one's id come from?
selfTest.a: Five, one per response record. The id is the `WARC-Record-ID` header of that record, read as `record_id` in FastWARC.

selfTest.q: Why can the same HTML give different training text under `main_content=True` and `main_content=False`, and which output is the better training data?
selfTest.a: The default keeps navigation, footer and sign-in text, and the main-content setting removes it and can also remove short real text such as a list item. Neither is better in general: it depends on what the page is and on what the model is for, so decide by reading samples and by an ablation, as FineWeb did, not by assumption.

selfTest.q: A page declares no charset and its bytes are Latin-1 text. What happens if you decode it as UTF-8 with `errors='replace'`, and what should the pipeline do instead?
selfTest.a: Bytes above 127 usually fail as UTF-8 and become replacement characters, so accented letters are lost silently. Fall back to a detected encoding, keep the encoding you used in the record, and count how often the fallback runs.

selfTest.q: Why is it a boundary bug to concatenate extracted documents into one file separated by blank lines?
selfTest.a: A blank line also occurs inside documents, so the original document boundaries cannot be recovered. Use an explicit record format with the id, or an end-of-document marker that cannot occur in the text, and test that the document count survives a write and read.

study.title: FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024)
study.locator: Section 3.3 (base filtering: a fastText English score of at least 0.65)
study.depth: Read only the language-filter sentence; the rest of 3.3 belongs to the quality-filter unit.

focus: The off-the-shelf identifier, `lid.176.bin`, returns a label and a probability for text on one line; it was trained on Wikipedia, Tatoeba and SETimes, and it knows 176 languages. A text in any other language still gets one of those labels.

A threshold such as 0.5 or 0.65 is a pipeline policy, not a property of the model. The score is not calibrated across languages, so measure retention per language on parallel or hand-labeled text before you fix the number.
Sample and audit: read labeled examples, count errors per slice, and report the error rate with an interval. Twenty samples can only bound an error rate loosely.

Normalization has two kinds of use. A matching key (for deduplication or contamination) may be aggressive because you keep the original. Stored training text should change only distinctions the standard says carry no meaning. NFKC does not meet that bar, which is Gopher's own conclusion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `identify(text)` that removes newlines, calls `predict(text, k=1)` on `lid.176.bin`, and returns `(code, score)`. Run it on the 1,012 `devtest` sentences of FLORES-200 (CC BY-SA 4.0) for English, Swahili, Yoruba and Shan, and tabulate top-1 accuracy, the share of sentences that are both correct and at least 0.65, and the mean score. In one run with fastText 0.9.2 (the `fasttext-numpy2-wheel` build) and `lid.176.bin`, English was 100% correct with 99.7% kept, Swahili 94.8% correct but only 28.7% kept, Yoruba 56.0% correct with 200 sentences labeled Irish, and every Shan sentence but one was labeled Burmese (mean score 0.89, since Shan is not among the 176). Then write what NFC and NFKC each do to `ﬁ` (U+FB01), the full-width `Ｈｅｌｌｏ` and `x²`, and say which result you could not undo.
traps: Reading the score as a probability of being right. Shan was labeled Burmese at a mean score of 0.89, and a short Norwegian Bokmål sentence (`Jeg bor i en liten by ved kysten og går til jobb hver dag.`) came back Danish at 0.96 in the same setup. A high score says the model is sure, not that it is correct.
Using one threshold for every language. A cutoff that keeps 99.7% of English can keep under a third of correctly identified Swahili, so a global rule silently removes a language from the corpus.

Cleaning the stored text with the same normalization you use for dedup keys. Lowercasing, accent stripping and whitespace collapse (the handout's MinHash step) are fine for a key; applied to the training text they erase case, diacritics and the indentation in code.

selfTest.q: A model is right on 94.8% of Swahili sentences, yet an English-tuned cutoff of 0.65 keeps 28.7% of them. What does this tell you about choosing a threshold?
selfTest.a: The score distribution differs by language, so one number trades very different amounts of recall per language. Choose the cutoff per language, or per slice, from a labeled sample, and report retention by language.

selfTest.q: You audit 300 sampled documents and find no language errors. What can you claim about the error rate?
selfTest.a: Only an upper bound: with 0 errors in 300 the two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound is about 1.2%, and the one-sided rule of three gives about 3/300 = 1%. You cannot claim zero, and the bound holds for the population you sampled from, not for slices you did not sample.

selfTest.q: Why can NFKC be used to build a deduplication key but should not be applied to the text you train on?
selfTest.a: NFKC replaces compatibility forms, for example `x²` becomes `x2` and ligatures and full-width letters become plain letters. A key only needs to treat such variants as equal, and the original stays available. Stored text would lose distinctions that math, code and typography rely on, and the change cannot be reversed from the output.

selfTest.q: A four-line Python function is labeled Swedish at 0.27. What does this say about running language identification on mixed web data?
selfTest.a: The identifier was trained on prose, so code, tables and markup get arbitrary labels and low scores. A language threshold would remove them as a side effect. Decide the domain first and route code and non-prose to their own rules.

study.locator: Section 4.4 with Table 4 (filter comparison) and Table 5 (reference data and threshold)
study.depth: Optional, after your own filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison. Read the numbers as that paper's results on its pool and recipe; do not compare its CORE scores with other papers' scores.

focus: Each rule is a guess about what bad text looks like, written for English prose. The handout implements four of Gopher's rules: word count, mean word length, lines ending in an ellipsis, and the share of words with a letter. The paper also has a stop-word test, a symbol-to-word ratio, a bullet-line rule and the repetition thresholds of Table A1.

A learned filter is a classifier of 'looks like the reference set', not of quality. The reference set decides what it learns: in DCLM Table 5 the choice of positive data moved CORE by more than five points at the same top-10% threshold (7B-1x scale, that paper's setup).

The threshold trades quantity for quality, and the right value depends on the token budget. The lecture's scale-dependent effects slide and the DCLM top-10% result both belong to one recipe, so a threshold from one run does not transfer.
The audit is the result. For every filter, keep the removed documents, sample them, and report the false-positive rate with an interval for each slice.
units.reproduce:
Closed-book, write `gopher_reason(text)` that returns `pass` or the name of the first failed rule: fewer than 50 or more than 100,000 words, mean word length outside 3 to 10, more than 30% of lines ending in `...`, fewer than 80% of words containing a letter, and fewer than two of the eight stop words `the be to of and that have with`. Run it on `"The city is on the banks of the river and has more than a hundred thousand people. " * 8` and on `"La ville est située au bord de la rivière et compte plus de cent mille habitants. " * 8`, then on `"def add(a, b):
    return a + b

" * 30`. Split words on whitespace: the English text passes, and the French text and the code fail only the stop-word rule. With `nltk.word_tokenize`, which the handout suggests, the code also fails the mean-word-length and alphabetic-share rules, so state your word split with the rules.
traps: Reading a passing test as evidence of quality. The handout's tests use constructed strings that each break one rule, so they check the thresholds and say nothing about false positives on real pages. `test_classify_quality` checks only two fixture texts.

Calling the handout's four rules 'the Gopher filter'. State the rules you ran. The stop-word test is the one that removes non-English text and code, so leaving it out changes what the filter does to a multilingual corpus.

Judging a filter on twenty examples, or scoring the classifier on pages it was trained on. One false positive in twenty gives an interval of about 0.1% to 25% (Clopper-Pearson), so the sample cannot tell a harmless filter from a harmful one. Audit more, per slice, and keep the audit sample out of training and out of threshold tuning.

selfTest.q: Why can the rule 'at least 80% of words contain an alphabetic character' remove good text?
selfTest.a: It assumes prose. Tables of numbers, math, data listings and symbol-heavy code fail it although they can be valuable training text. It is a statement about the kind of text you want, which should match the corpus purpose.

selfTest.q: A classifier is trained with pages linked from Wikipedia as positives and random crawl pages as negatives. What does it learn, and where will it fail?
selfTest.a: It learns what separates those two samples: style, topic and source type. It will score low on good text unlike the references (forum answers, code, other languages) and can score high on reference-shaped text that is wrong. Its score has meaning only after you check it against labeled samples.

selfTest.q: You audit 20 removed documents and 1 was a false positive. What can you report?
selfTest.a: An observed rate of 5%, with a 95% interval of roughly 0.1% to 25%. Twenty documents cannot separate 1% from 20%, so sample more and report per slice.

selfTest.q: A top-10% threshold gave the best model in one paper. Why is that not a rule for your pipeline?
selfTest.a: The threshold trades data quantity for quality, so the best value depends on the token budget, the pool and the reference set. A longer run wants more, lower-scoring data. Tune it on your own comparison at your own budget.

units.title: Exact deduplication and MinHash near-deduplication thresholds
outcomes: Derive the probability \(1 - (1 - s^r)^b\) that two documents with Jaccard similarity \(s\) share a bucket, and the threshold \((1/b)^{1/r}\) where it rises, then choose \(b\) and \(r\) for a target similarity.
Implement exact line deduplication and MinHash-LSH document deduplication that verifies each candidate pair with exact Jaccard, clusters duplicates and keeps one document by a fixed rule.
State what the shingle size, the threshold and the scope of deduplication (per snapshot or global) trade, and keep a record of each duplicate cluster.
units.why: Duplicates waste training tokens, inflate memorization, and let evaluation text leak into training. MinHash lets you find near-duplicates without comparing every pair, but its parameters are easy to get wrong by a factor that the code never reports.

study.title: datasketch: MinHash LSH
study.locator: 'Retrieval characteristics and parameter tuning' and 'Common Issues with MinHash LSH' (page read 2026-10-16, datasketch 2.0.0)

focus: Fix three choices before you code: the item that is compared (line, paragraph, document or n-gram span), the match rule (exact, shared piece, fraction shared), and the action (drop all, keep one). Exact dedup is a hash of the normalized item; equal hashes are a candidate until the bytes are compared.

MinHash gives \(P[h(A) = h(B)] = J(A, B)\) for one random hash. With \(k = b \cdot r\) hashes split into \(b\) bands of \(r\) rows, two documents collide if any band matches, which has probability \(1 - (1 - s^r)^b\). More rows per band raises the threshold, more bands lowers it.

LSH proposes candidates and does not decide. Check each candidate with exact Jaccard on the shingles, as the handout does, then cluster by connected components and keep one document per cluster by a fixed rule. Normalize only for the key (the handout lists lowercasing, punctuation, whitespace, accents and NFD) and keep the raw text and the cluster record.

The threshold is a modeling choice. Lee et al. use word 5-grams with a Jaccard test at 0.8 followed by an edit-similarity test at 0.8, Gopher uses 13-grams at 0.8, FineWeb uses 5-grams targeting about 75%, and FineWeb found that deduplicating each snapshot separately beat deduplicating all of them together.
units.reproduce: Derive \(P = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b\) and the threshold \((1/b)^{1/r}\). Then compute, with 9000 hashes as Lee et al. arrange them (450 bands of 20 rows, their Appendix A), the threshold and \(P\) at \(s = 0.8\); repeat for 20 bands of 450 rows as the lecture example reads them; and for 100 hashes in 10 bands (the first MinHash test in the handout) at \(s = 0.8\). Expect a threshold of about 0.737 and \(P \approx 0.995\); a threshold of about 0.993 and \(P\) about \(5 \times 10^{-43}\); and \(P \approx 0.679\).
traps: Lee et al. name the parameters the other way round from the lecture and the handout. Their Section 4.2 writes \(1 - (1 - s^b)^r\) with \(b = 20\) hashes per bucket and \(r = 450\) buckets, which is 450 bands of 20 rows. The lecture's code puts 20 bands of 450 rows through \((1/b)^{1/r}\) and gets a threshold near 0.99, where two documents at \(s = 0.8\) essentially never collide. Always check which variable counts bands and test the result against the target similarity.

Treating a library threshold as a hard cutoff. `MinHashLSH(threshold=0.9, num_perm=128)` in datasketch 2.0.0 picks 5 bands of 25 rows, and `threshold=0.5` picks 25 bands of 5 rows, by balancing false positives and false negatives. It returns candidates; keep the exact Jaccard check.

Believing that more deduplication is always better. FineWeb's global MinHash removed up to 90% of the oldest snapshots and left worse text than it removed, and Lee et al. note that train and test duplicates must be handled on purpose (they kept the copy in the evaluation set).

selfTest.q: A 128-hash signature is split as 16 bands of 8 rows, or as 8 bands of 16 rows. Which setup has the lower threshold, and what does the lower threshold cost?
selfTest.a: 16 bands of 8 rows: its threshold is \((1/16)^{1/8} \approx 0.707\), against \((1/8)^{1/16} \approx 0.878\). The lower threshold raises recall and also produces more candidate pairs, so more exact checks and, if you skip them, more false positives.

selfTest.q: With 10 bands of 10 rows, what is the chance that documents at \(s = 0.9\) collide, and at \(s = 0.5\)?
selfTest.a: At \(s = 0.9\): \(1 - (1 - 0.9^{10})^{10} \approx 0.986\). At \(s = 0.5\): about 0.0097. That is small for one pair but not for a corpus: with a million documents there are about \(5 \times 10^{11}\) pairs, so even rare collisions give many candidates to verify.

selfTest.q: Two different documents hash to the same value in exact deduplication, here with a 1-bit hash. What must the algorithm do?
selfTest.a: Treat the hash only as a bucket key and compare the normalized text inside the bucket, keeping both documents when the texts differ. Dropping on a hash match alone silently deletes distinct documents.

selfTest.q: FineWeb's globally deduplicated data trained a model barely better than the undeduplicated data. Name one reason the paper gives.
selfTest.a: Global deduplication removed most of the older snapshots, and the part it kept was worse text (more ads and keyword lists) than the part it removed. Removing duplicates also removes the many repeats of good pages, so what remains need not be better. Per-snapshot deduplication gave the improvement.

study.depth: Optional. Read how the match is defined (the question text plus one answer option, and only the last sentence of long MMLU questions) and the authors' remark that this still gives many false positives.

focus: Contamination is overlap between one named evaluation set and your training text, and the unit of overlap depends on the task. A 13-gram test on whole documents cannot see a six-word question. Compare the designs: Gopher (whole-document 13-gram Jaccard), Tulu 3 (8-grams, prompts only, token coverage), DCLM (question plus an answer option).

Use containment, not Jaccard, when a short item may sit inside a long page: Jaccard divides by the union and the page dominates it. Count the share of the item's tokens or n-grams found in the training text.

A detector reports what it can see. Paraphrases and answer-only text have no shared n-grams with the question, and an item with fewer than n tokens cannot match at all. Report 'no verbatim overlap at n = 8', not 'clean', and review every match by hand.

PII and harm filters are precision-recall trades. Dolma masks only emails, IP addresses and phone numbers because regexes find those with high precision; its two toxicity thresholds removed 5.5% to 7.3% of content or 29.1% to 34.9%. Dodge shows a word list removing text from and about minority groups at unequal rates, so report removal by slice.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `coverage(test, train, n)` that returns the share of the test item's lowercase `\w+` tokens lying inside at least one n-gram that also occurs in the training text. Use n = 8 on `Maria has 12 apples and buys 15 more at the market. She gives 9 apples to her neighbour. How many apples does Maria have now?` against four training texts: the item inside a longer page, a copy with 12, 15 and 9 changed to 14, 17 and 11, a copy with `local` inserted before `market`, and a paraphrase. You should get 1.0, 0.44, 1.0 and 0.0. Say which of the four a rule 'more than 50% covered' flags, and what the numbers become at n = 4 (1.0, 0.68, 1.0, 0.0) and n = 13 (1.0, 0.0, 0.6, 0.0).
traps: Choosing the match unit from the dataset you have read about instead of from the evaluation items. With the Maria item inside a page of 200 filler sentences, 13-gram Jaccard is below 0.01 while containment is 1.0, so a Jaccard-above-0.8 rule would miss a verbatim copy; and an item of fewer than n tokens never matches any n-gram at all, so add an exact normalized full-string check.

Reading zero matches as 'not contaminated'. The detector sees surface overlap only: the paraphrase scored 0.0 in the reproduce step, an answer-only passage shares no n-gram with its question, and the changed-number copy fell below the 50% rule at n = 8. State what the detector cannot establish, and review a sample of matches and of near-misses.

Storing the evidence in a way that recreates the harm. An audit file of raw emails and phone numbers is itself a PII leak, so store the type, offsets, a keyed hash and a masked excerpt. Also keep the unmasked counts: a mask string such as `|||EMAIL_ADDRESS|||` can already occur in the text, and only real emails should be counted.

selfTest.q: A training page contains an evaluation question verbatim among 200 other sentences. Why does a 'Jaccard above 0.8 on 13-grams' rule miss it, and what would catch it?
selfTest.a: The union of n-grams is dominated by the page, so the Jaccard similarity is tiny (below 0.01 for the Maria item in a 200-sentence page). The share of the question's n-grams that appear in the page, its containment, is 1.0 and would catch it.

selfTest.q: An evaluation item has six words and you check 8-grams. What happens, and what do you do?
selfTest.a: The item has no 8-grams, so it can never be flagged and the check passes silently. Add an exact match on the normalized full item, or a smaller n with manual review, for items shorter than n.

selfTest.q: With n = 8, a copy of a math problem with three changed numbers has 44% token coverage. Does a 50% rule flag it, and does it matter?
selfTest.a: No, it is just below the rule. It matters because the problem structure and its solution pattern are still in the training text. Use a lower coverage threshold or a number-masked comparison and review the matches; the right threshold depends on the item length and the number of edits.

selfTest.q: Why does Dolma mask only emails, IP addresses and phone numbers?
selfTest.a: Those can be matched with regular expressions at high precision and web-scale speed. Names and addresses need a model-based detector, which is slower and less precise. The cost is recall: anything the patterns miss stays in the data, so the card should say so.

selfTest.q: A word-list filter removes 6.2% of one group's documents and 42% of another's, as estimated by a dialect model. What does an overall removal rate of, say, 8% hide?
selfTest.a: It hides the unequal removal by group. The corpus would underrepresent the second group's text, which counts as a loss if that group is in the population stated in the corpus purpose. Report removal by slice and review a sample of removed text per slice.

study.locator: Milestone E (measurement) and the 'Measurement requirements': compression and fertility by slice, and the effect of vocabulary and packing on sequence length, embedding parameters and KV memory

focus: Fertility is tokens per word, and it needs a definition of word. Whitespace splitting gives 13 tokens per 'word' for Chinese in the run below, so use parallel text: the same sentences in two languages, and the ratio of token counts (Petrov's premium).

Bytes per token is not comparable across scripts, because an unaccented Latin letter takes 1 byte, a Cyrillic letter 2 and a Devanagari or Han character 3. Under the Qwen3 tokenizer Russian shows more bytes per token than English and still needs 1.75 times the tokens.

The premium changes the budget. A fixed context window holds \(1/\text{premium}\) of the content, a fixed training-token budget buys the same fraction, and a loss per token cannot be compared between tokenizers. Compare bits per byte of the same held-out text instead.

FLORES-200 is translated encyclopedic and news text, so it measures that domain. Web text, code and your own domain differ, and a tokenizer trained on other languages falls back to bytes: GPT-2 averaged 1.00 bytes per token on Tamil and 1.03 on Shan in the run below.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for the 1,012 FLORES-200 `devtest` sentences of English, French, Hindi, Tamil, Thai and Simplified Chinese, encode each sentence with `encode(s, add_special_tokens=False)` and compute the premium as total tokens divided by the English total, for GPT-2 and for the Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer. In one run (transformers 5.19.0, tokenizers 0.23.3, `gpt2` revision 607a30d783dfa663caf39e06633721c8d4cfcd7e, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` revision c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca) the premiums were, for GPT-2 then Qwen3: French 2.00 and 1.58, Hindi 7.41 and 4.42, Tamil 15.54 and 6.11, Thai 8.99 and 2.55, Chinese 3.15 and 1.00. Report your own table with the median of the per-sentence ratios beside each total.
traps: Reporting tokens per word for every language. In the same run Qwen3 gave 13.4 tokens per whitespace-separated unit for Chinese, 16.4 for Thai and 35.8 for Japanese, because those texts have few spaces. The number is a property of the splitter, not of the tokenizer.

Comparing bytes per token across languages, or loss per token across tokenizers. Both change when the unit changes, so they can rank languages or models the wrong way round. Use token counts on parallel text for languages and bits per byte on a shared held-out set for models.

Trusting the premium of one tokenizer for another or for another domain. The same sentences cost GPT-2 7.41 times the English tokens in Hindi and Qwen3 4.42 times. On one Python file (`tests/test_deduplication.py` from CS336 Assignment 4, 133 lines), GPT-2 gave 2.21 bytes per token and Qwen3 gave 4.81, against about 4.7 to 4.8 for the English `devtest` text in both.

selfTest.q: A tokenizer has a premium of 4.42 for Hindi relative to English. What does that mean for a fixed 8,192-token context and for a fixed training-token budget?
selfTest.a: The context holds about 1/4.42, or 23%, of the English content, and a budget split equally by tokens gives Hindi about 23% as much content as English. Both follow from counting in tokens.

selfTest.q: Under one tokenizer, Russian shows 5.37 bytes per token and English 4.78, yet Russian needs 1.75 times the tokens for the same sentences. How?
selfTest.a: A Cyrillic letter takes two UTF-8 bytes against one for a Latin letter, so each Russian token carries more bytes but fewer letters of content. Bytes per token is not normalized by content; the premium on parallel text is.

selfTest.q: Why is 'tokens per word' a poor fertility measure for Chinese, Japanese and Thai?
selfTest.a: Those scripts do not separate words with spaces, so a whitespace 'word' is a whole clause and the ratio is about the splitter. Use tokens per character, or the ratio of token counts on parallel text.

selfTest.q: A model with a larger vocabulary reports a lower per-token validation loss than a baseline. Can you say it models the text better?
selfTest.a: No. The two models split the same text into different numbers of tokens, so the losses average over different units. Convert both to bits per byte (or per character) on the same held-out text, then compare.

study.locator: Section 8 'From Tokenize to Training Stream', 8.1 'Sequence Packing' (the first-fit-decreasing cell) and 8.2 'Block-Diagonal Attention Mask' (the mask cell)
study.depth: Skip 8.3 on fill-in-the-middle. The notebook says position ids must restart for every document; with rotary positions they need not, as the reproduce step shows.

focus: Two masks, two jobs. The attention mask says which earlier tokens a position may read; the loss mask says which positions have a valid target. The position that holds an end-of-document token predicts the first token of the next document, which its own document cannot predict. Pipelines differ here: the Assignment 5 supplement trains on every packed position, others mask that one, so choose and record it. Padding positions are always masked.

With a plain causal mask a token in the second document attends to the first. Zhao et al. train 1.3B models on the same 150B tokens with and without intra-document masking, and the masked model has the lowest average perplexity: 8.410 against 9.172 at 2K context and 8.079 against 9.065 at 8K (Table 1).

With rotary position embeddings the attention score depends only on the offset between two positions, so a document's logits are the same whether its positions start at 0 or at its offset in the sequence, up to floating-point error. Zhao et al. apply rotary embeddings before the variable-length attention call and do not reset positions. With learned absolute positions you must reset them.

Decide the tail and truncation rules and record them: Gopher drops the final short chunk, and a document longer than the context is split. A document continued in the next sequence has lost its beginning, so keep each span's `doc_id`, start and end offsets.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, build a 2-layer decoder with rotary positions (model width 32, 4 heads, a 50-token vocabulary, `torch.manual_seed(0)`) and pack document A (6 tokens), an end token, document B (5 tokens) and an end token. Build a plain causal mask and an intra-document mask from per-token document ids (the end token belongs to the document it closes). Show that replacing A changes B's logits under the causal mask (max absolute difference about 0.4 in the run, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU) and changes nothing under the intra-document mask (0.0). Then show that B's logits from the packed intra-document run match B run alone with `torch.allclose(a, b, atol=1e-5)`, while `torch.equal` is `False` (max absolute difference 3.6e-07), and that resetting positions per document changes them by at most about 2e-07.
traps: Testing equality with `==` or `torch.equal`. A packed batch and a single document run different matrix shapes, so the results differ in the last bits; assert closeness with a tolerance, and assert exact zero only for the case where one document's tokens are replaced inside the same packed run.

Building the attention mask and forgetting the loss mask, so that padding tokens count in the loss denominator, or the end-token position is trained on the next document's first token when your design meant to mask it.

Treating a continued document as a new one. When a long document is split across two sequences, the second part starts mid-document with no left context; mark it as a continuation in the span record so that later counts of documents and tokens stay correct.

selfTest.q: Two documents are packed in one sequence with a plain causal mask. Does changing the first document's tokens change the loss on the second? Which mask removes the effect?
selfTest.a: Yes: every token of the second document can attend to the first, so its hidden states depend on it. A block-diagonal causal mask built from the document ids removes the dependence, which the swap test above checks.

selfTest.q: Should the loss at the position holding the end token be kept in packed pretraining?
selfTest.a: It is a design choice to record. Its target is the first token of the next document, which the current document cannot predict, so under an intra-document mask that position can only learn how documents tend to begin. Many pipelines keep it (the Assignment 5 supplement trains on every position) and others mask it. If you mask it, the model still learns to emit the end token, because that is the target at the previous position, whose loss is kept.

selfTest.q: Why do the logits of a document not change when its rotary positions start at an offset instead of 0?
selfTest.a: The rotary score of a query and key depends only on the difference of their positions, which is unchanged by a common offset, so within one document the attention scores are the same up to rounding. A learned absolute embedding depends on the position itself, so there the offset matters.

selfTest.q: Zhao et al. report intra-document masking lowers perplexity at both context lengths. What does that not show?
selfTest.a: It shows this effect for 1.3B models on 150B tokens of one corpus (SlimPajama), measured on documents scored one at a time. It does not show the size of the effect for other models or data, nor that the masking is free: they measured a 4% slowdown with FlashAttention-2, and much larger ones with an explicit mask.

study.locator: Appendix A.1.2 step 6: sequences are drawn from the subsets according to fixed weights

focus: State weights in tokens of one named tokenizer. Sampling documents 50/50 from a source of 100-token documents and one of 1,000-token documents gives a token share of 9.1% and 90.9%, not 50/50.

The exponent \(\alpha\) interpolates: \(\alpha = 1\) is proportional to size, \(\alpha = 0\) is uniform. With a 1T-token budget, a 10T-token source and a 10B-token source, uniform sampling reads the large one for 0.05 epochs and the small one for 50 epochs, which the lecture flags as overfitting risk.

Repetition is not free and not worthless. Muennighoff et al. model effective data as \(D' = U_D + U_D R_D^{*} (1 - e^{-R_D / R_D^{*}})\) where \(U_D\) is the unique tokens and \(R_D\) the number of repeats; with their fitted \(R_D^{*} \approx 15.4\) each token of a 4-epoch run is worth about 0.93 of a fresh one, and of a 40-epoch run about 0.38. That is a fit to their models, data and setup.

A mixture that is best for a small run is not best for a large one, because epochs scale with the budget. Cap epochs per source (UniMax) or simulate the large run's epochs at small scale. Treat synthetic text as its own source with a recorded generator, and sample it under the same cap.
units.reproduce: Derive the expected epochs of source \(i\) as \(T p_i / n_i\). Then, for \(n = (10^{13}, 10^{10})\) tokens and \(T = 10^{12}\), compute \(p\) and the epochs for \(\alpha = 1\), \(0.5\) and \(0\). Expect \(p = (0.999, 0.001)\) with 0.1 epochs each; \(p = (0.969, 0.031)\) with epochs (0.097, 3.07); and \(p = (0.5, 0.5)\) with epochs (0.05, 50). Then cap each source at 4 epochs by giving the small source 4 epochs (\(4 \times 10^{10}\) tokens, \(p = 0.04\)) and the rest to the large one, and compute \(D'/U_D\) for 4 epochs with \(R_D^{*} = 15.39\), which is 3.73.
traps: Reading 'effective tokens' the same way in every source. In the notebook it means raw tokens times epochs; in Muennighoff et al. it means tokens counted by value, which is less than the tokens processed once data repeats. Write which one you mean in every table.

Treating the four-epoch result as a safe rule. It came from fixed-compute runs of models up to 9B parameters on subsets of C4 (with a check on OSCAR in an appendix), and the fitted curve says each repeated token is already worth a bit less. Check it for your model size and data, and check that filtering did not make your small source even smaller.

Tuning weights on a small run and applying them at scale. A weight of 0.9 on a 10B-token source is 0.9 epochs at a 10B-token budget and 90 epochs at 1T, so the small-run optimum silently becomes an overfitting recipe.

selfTest.q: Two sources have 100 and 400 tokens, the budget is 1,000 tokens, and \(\alpha = 1\). What are the probabilities, tokens and epochs? What changes at \(\alpha = 0\)?
selfTest.a: \(p = (0.2, 0.8)\), tokens (200, 800), epochs (2, 2). At \(\alpha = 0\), \(p = (0.5, 0.5)\), tokens (500, 500) and epochs (5, 1.25): the small source is repeated four times more often than the large one.

selfTest.q: Source A has 1,000 documents of 100 tokens and source B has 1,000 documents of 1,000 tokens. You sample documents with probability 0.5 each. What are the token shares?
selfTest.a: A gets \(0.5 \times 100 = 50\) and B gets \(0.5 \times 1000 = 500\) tokens per draw, so the shares are 9.1% and 90.9%. To get 50/50 in tokens, weight by tokens or sample so that the expected token counts match.

selfTest.q: Using the fitted repetition curve, what share of the processed tokens of a source repeated for 40 epochs counts as effective?
selfTest.a: About 38%: \(D'/U_D = 1 + 15.39 (1 - e^{-39/15.39}) \approx 15.2\) against 40 tokens processed per unique token. The curve flattens at \(1 + R_D^{*} \approx 16.4\) unique-token equivalents, so more epochs add almost nothing.

selfTest.q: A small run finds the best weight for a scarce source is 0.9. Why might that fail at 100 times the tokens?
selfTest.a: Epochs of the source scale with the budget, so 100 times more tokens means 100 times more epochs over the same source. What was a good weight at 0.9 epochs becomes about 90 epochs of repetition, past the point where repeats help.

study.locator: Appendix A.1.2 'Constructing Token Sequences' (p. 42), steps 1 to 7 from drawing a document to shuffling and batching

focus: Make position a value, not a hidden state. If the order of epoch \(e\) is a function of the seed and \(e\) alone, for example `np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64([seed, epoch])).permutation(n)`, then batch \(k\) is the slice \([kB, (k+1)B)\) of it and a resume needs only the epoch and step. A single random generator shared across epochs needs replaying to reach epoch 2.

Shard by a stable hash of the document id and list the result in the manifest. Python's built-in `hash` of a string differs between processes, and changing the shard count moves most documents, so a shard is a manifest entry and not a directory listing.
Resume has to give each record exactly once. The documented tip says that with `.shuffle()` the examples in the shuffle buffer are lost on resume; the reproduce step measures how many.

Lineage is a join. Keep one record per packed sequence with its `(doc_id, start, end)` spans, join on the stable `source` and `id` pair, and build the inverse index from document to steps so that a deletion or contamination finding can name the batches and checkpoints affected.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write `batch(version, seed, epoch, step)` that returns the `(doc_id, start, end)` spans of that batch, taking the order of sequences from `np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64([seed, epoch])).permutation(n_sequences)`. Show that a run resumed at step 61 reproduces steps 61 onward of an uninterrupted run exactly (1,003 sequences, batch size 8, 125 steps, 3 sequences unused per epoch). Assign documents `doc-000000` to `doc-019999` to shards with the first eight bytes of a SHA-256 digest modulo \(K\), and show that only 20.0% keep their shard when \(K\) goes from 4 to 5. Then break it twice: use the built-in `hash` and see the assignment change between fresh processes (in one run `hash('doc-000001') % 4` gave 3, 0, 1, 3, 0, 3 over six processes), and resume a shuffled Hugging Face `IterableDataset`.
traps: Losing records on resume while the loss looks fine. With datasets 5.1.0, a dataset of 40 rows in 4 shards, `shuffle(seed=7, buffer_size=8)` and an interruption after 13 rows, the resumed run skipped 5 rows and repeated 1. Only a comparison of document ids with an uninterrupted run shows it.

Letting worker count change the data. If every worker shuffles its own shards, the content of batch \(k\) depends on the number of workers and a rerun on other hardware gives different batches. Define batch content globally and let workers only fetch.

Forgetting the unused tail. A partial last batch that is dropped means some sequences are not seen in that epoch, and with a new permutation each epoch it is a different set each time. Write the dropped sequence ids into the lineage record, or you cannot say that every document was seen.

selfTest.q: Why does computing the epoch order from `(seed, epoch)` make resuming cheap, while one generator shared across epochs does not?
selfTest.a: The permutation of any epoch can be recomputed directly, so a resume needs only the epoch and step. With one shared generator, the state at epoch 2 exists only after the earlier permutations have consumed it, so you must either store the generator state or replay the epochs, and a fresh generator gives a different permutation.

selfTest.q: Documents are assigned to shards by a hash modulo \(K\). You change \(K\) from 4 to 5. What happens, and what does it mean for lineage?
selfTest.a: About four in five documents move to another shard (20.0% stayed in the run above). Any record that names a shard becomes wrong, so lineage should refer to document ids and the manifest version, and a change of shard count must create a new dataset version.

selfTest.q: The loss jumps after a resume. Name three data-side causes you can check from lineage.
selfTest.a: The shuffle buffer or other loader state was lost, so records are missing or repeated; the epoch, seed or worker count differs, so the order changed; or the dataset version or tail handling differs. Compare the document ids of steps \(k\) to \(k+m\) of the resumed run with those of an uninterrupted run.

selfTest.q: A document must be removed. How do you find which batches and checkpoints are affected?
selfTest.a: Invert the lineage: document id to the sequences that contain its spans, to the (epoch, step) of each such sequence, to the first checkpoint saved after the earliest of those steps. The index must keep the dropped-tail sequences too, or you will miss documents that were never trained on.

focus: A version is its content, not its name or its date. Hash every file, sort the entries, include the configuration that produced the files, and hash that list; reordering or touching files then changes nothing, and one changed byte does.

Derived data is regenerated, not trusted. Record the raw input versions, the code commit, the filter and tokenizer versions and the seeds, then check that deleting the derived files and rebuilding gives the same manifest.

The card states purpose, sources and rights, transformations with removal rates per stage, sampling and mixture, known gaps, contamination and PII findings, and uses to avoid. Every number belongs to a named tokenizer and a dataset version.
A checkpoint stores the dataset version, the tokenizer identity and the loader position. Resume and evaluation compare them with the manifest and fail loudly when they differ.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `build_manifest(root, config)` that returns a version id: the SHA-256 of a sorted list of `[relative_path, size, file_sha256]` entries together with the configuration, serialized with sorted keys. In a small test show that a copy written in another order with other modification times has the same id, that changing one byte of one file changes it, and that changing `seed` in the configuration changes it. Then write a `verify(manifest, root)` that recomputes it, and a `resume(checkpoint, manifest)` that raises when the checkpoint's `data_version` differs.
traps: Versioning by directory name or date. `data_v3` says nothing about its bytes, and two runs with that label can differ. Name the version by the content hash and keep the label as a convenience.

Leaving out the pieces that change the result: the tokenizer revision, the filter thresholds, the sampler seed and the contamination reference sets. A manifest of files alone cannot tell you why two corpora from the same files trained differently.

Writing the card once, at release. Counts go stale when a stage is rerun, and the card must quote the dataset version it describes. Regenerate the numbers from the manifest and the stage logs instead of typing them.

selfTest.q: Why does the version id hash the sorted list of file entries rather than the modification times or the archive of the files?
selfTest.a: Modification times and archive layout change when the same bytes are rewritten, which would give a new version for identical data. Sorted path, size and content hash depend only on the data, so the id is stable across copies and changes when any byte changes.

selfTest.q: Two corpora were built from identical raw files and trained different models. Which manifest fields would you compare first?
selfTest.a: The configuration and code commit: filter thresholds, language-ID and quality-model versions, the tokenizer revision, the mixture weights and the seeds. Identical inputs with different processing parameters give different corpora.

selfTest.q: A token count in a card says 3 billion. What else must the card state for that number to mean anything?
selfTest.a: The tokenizer and its revision, and the dataset version. Token counts depend on the tokenizer: the same text has a different count under another one, as the premium measurements showed.

selfTest.q: What should happen when you try to evaluate a checkpoint whose recorded dataset version differs from the one in your manifest?
selfTest.a: The run should stop with an error that names both versions, not continue with a warning. A silent mismatch makes every later comparison about different data.
